column4: The verse's seed yields seven ears, a specific image of growth multiplying from what is sown; this adds a crop-growth parallel to the section's plant emerging from earth, though its point is charitable giving.
The verse pictures a fertile garden on a height receiving heavy rain or drizzle and yielding fruit, a specific soil-and-rain counterpart to the section's pasture emerging under rain.

The verse's flourishing garden is struck by a fiery whirlwind and burned; this is a concrete reversal of the section's rain-fed green growth, though the cause is sudden fire rather than natural drying.
This preceding verse spreads the earth and names rivers and paired fruits; it supplies the earth-and-fruit setting continued by 13:4's gardens and crops.
The good word is compared to a good tree with firm roots and branches reaching skyward, joining the section's rooted emergence to its vertical sky-to-pasture image.
The tree yields fruit by its Lord's permission; this gives a recurring, sustained counterpart to the section's pasture and its root-family image of a cloud that nurtures plants.
The bad word is compared to a tree uprooted from the earth with no stability, a specific plant reversal beside the section's growth from soil and its later debris.
The verse says rain from the sky makes the earth green, a direct compact formulation of the section's cloud-to-rain-to-pasture scene.
This next verse adds the olive tree of Mount Sinai, yielding oil and food, to the date, grape, and garden produce named in 23:19.

The word نُرَبِّكَ is from the source section's root ر ب ب in the explicit nurturing sense: Pharaoh says he raised Moses as a child. The section links that root-family to a cloud that nurtures plants, extending the sustaining image to human upbringing.

This verse says that when God calls people from the earth they come forth; the source section's root خ ر ج describes pasture brought out from earth, and here the same extraction image points to resurrection.
After 30:50 describes revived earth, this verse presents a wind and something seen yellow; it gives the rain-revived scene its specific yellowing reversal.
The verse answers who can revive decayed bones: the one who created them first. Its contribution is the resurrection claim, followed in 36:80 by a green-tree-and-fire sign.
The verse asks who made the tree from which people kindle fire; green vegetation thus yields fire, joining the section's pasture cycle to the later Fire image in Surah 87.
The verse says herbs and trees prostrate; alongside Surah 87's opening command to glorify the Most High, it makes vegetation itself part of the worship scene.
This adjacent verse says the heaven was raised and balance set, carrying the sky-and-earth frame of 55:6 into the section's vertical image from above to pasture.
The passage next says the earth was laid out for living creatures, giving the ground beneath the section's emerging pasture its place in the created order.
This continuation names fruit and date palms, extending the earth's produce scene beyond the pasture.
The verse adds grain and fragrant plants, a specific crop-and-herb counterpart to the section's grass and grazing.
The two gardens of Paradise have gushing springs, a lasting garden scene that marks a boundary against the section's pasture that dries and is carried away.
This garden passage names fruit, date palms, and pomegranates; it continues the unwithering produce scene begun in 55:64.

After the surah's images of prostrating plants, raised heaven, earth, fruit, and dark gardens, this closing verse blesses the name of the Lord, echoing the section's opening “name of your Lord” across a botanical and celestial sequence.
The verse asks people to consider the fire they kindle; it opens the adjacent creation passage in which 56:72 identifies the tree from which fire is made.
The verse asks who made the tree that supplies kindling; it specifically joins plant growth to fire, a reversal of the section's green pasture and a bridge to Surah 87's Fire.
The continuation calls that fire a reminder and provision for travelers, joining the tree-to-fire image to the section's movement from the plant cycle toward reminder.
The verse says the people of the Fire have only thorny ضَرِيع for food; this is a specific boundary to the section's pasture as grazing and provision.
The next verse says that food neither nourishes nor relieves hunger, contrasting the pasture's sustaining growth with the Fire's barren provision.
